title: THE WOLF AND THE KID
content: There was once a little Kid whose growing horns made him think he was a grown-up Goat and able to take care of himself. So one evening when the flock started home from the pasture and his mother called, the Kid paid no attention and kept right on eating. The next thing he knew, he was all alone. The sun was sinking fast, and shadows were creeping over the field. Just then a Wolf came out from the bushes nearby, looking for a nice supper. The Kid knew there wasn’t much hope, but he tried calling out, 'Please, Mr. Wolf, I know you’re going to eat me. But first, could you play a song on your pipe for me to dance to?' The Wolf liked the idea of a little music before eating, so he played a tune. The Kid started dancing, and the noise woke up some Dogs nearby who ran out barking. The Wolf had to drop his pipe and run off to save himself. 'That’s what I get for trying to be a musician,' grumbled the Wolf as he dashed away. Moral: Don’t get distracted from what you’re good at.

title: THE TORTOISE AND THE DUCKS
content: The Tortoise, you know, carries his house on his back. No matter how hard he tries, he can’t leave home. They say he got tired of this and told the Ducks he wanted to see the world. The Ducks were kind and said they’d help him. They found a strong stick and told the Tortoise to bite it hard in the middle. Then each Duck grabbed an end of the stick with their beaks and flew up into the air. The Tortoise held on tight as they carried him high above the fields and rivers. He was amazed at the view and couldn’t help saying, 'I’m the king of the sky!' But when he opened his mouth to speak, he let go of the stick and fell all the way down to the ground, smashing into pieces. Moral: Keep your mouth shut when you’re in a risky spot.

title: THE YOUNG CRAB AND HIS MOTHER
content: One day, a Mother Crab said to her Young Crab, 'Why do you walk sideways like that? You should walk straight ahead with your toes pointed out.' The Young Crab replied, 'Show me how, Mom, and I’ll do it.' So the Mother Crab tried to walk straight, but she could only go sideways too. When she saw she couldn’t do it, she said, 'Well, I guess you’re right to walk your own way.' Moral: Don’t tell others to do what you can’t do yourself.

title: THE FROGS AND THE OX
content: An Ox came down to a pond to drink and accidentally stepped on a young Frog, squashing him flat. The other Frogs ran to tell their mother what happened. 'Oh Mother,' they cried, 'a huge beast stepped on little brother and killed him!' 'How big was it?' she asked. 'Was it this big?' And she puffed herself up a little. 'No, much bigger,' they said. So she puffed up more and asked, 'This big?' 'No, way bigger!' they shouted. She kept puffing herself up bigger and bigger until suddenly she burst. Moral: Don’t try to be something you’re not.

title: THE DOG, THE COCK, AND THE FOX
content: A Dog and a Cock became friends and decided to travel together. At night, the Cock perched in a tree while the Dog slept at the bottom. When morning came, the Cock crowed loudly as usual. A Fox heard it and ran over, thinking he’d get an easy meal. He called up to the Cock, 'That’s a beautiful song! Come down and let’s chat.' The Cock said, 'Sure, just wake up my friend down there, and he’ll let you in.' The Fox went to the tree trunk and started barking, but the Dog jumped up and chased him away. Moral: Smart friends can outsmart a trickster.

title: THE EAGLE AND THE JACKDAW
content: An Eagle swooped down and grabbed a Lamb to carry off to her nest. A Jackdaw saw this and thought he could do the same. So he flew down, grabbed a big Ram, and tried to lift it. But his claws got stuck in the Ram’s wool, and he couldn’t get free. The Shepherd came along, caught the Jackdaw, and clipped his wings. He gave the bird to his kids as a pet. 'What kind of bird is this?' they asked. 'It’s a Jackdaw,' said the Shepherd, 'but he thought he was an Eagle.' Moral: Know your limits.

title: THE BOY AND THE FILBERTS
content: A Boy stuck his hand into a jar of Filberts and grabbed as many as he could. But when he tried to pull his hand out, it was too full to fit through the neck of the jar. He didn’t want to let go of any nuts, so he just stood there crying. A man passing by said, 'Take less, and you’ll get your hand out.' The Boy dropped half the nuts and pulled his hand free. Moral: Don’t be too greedy, or you’ll end up with nothing.

title: THE FARMER AND THE SNAKE
content: One winter, a Farmer found a Snake nearly frozen in the cold. He felt sorry for it, picked it up, and warmed it against his chest. As soon as the Snake woke up and felt better, it bit the Farmer, who fell down dying. With his last breath, he said, 'I should’ve known better than to help something so mean.' Moral: Some things will hurt you no matter how kind you are.

title: THE FARMER AND HIS SONS
content: A Farmer was about to die and wanted his Sons to keep working the farm. He called them over and said, 'I’ve hidden a treasure somewhere in the fields. Dig for it after I’m gone.' When he died, the Sons dug up every inch of the land looking for gold. They didn’t find any treasure, but all that digging made the soil so good that the next harvest was huge and made them rich. Moral: Hard work is its own reward.

title: THE DONKEY AND THE LAP DOG
content: A Farmer had a Donkey and a little Lap Dog. The Lap Dog would jump into the Farmer’s lap, get petted, and eat scraps from the table. The Donkey, watching from the barn, got jealous. One day, he broke free, ran into the house, and tried to climb into the Farmer’s lap. He brayed and kicked, breaking everything around him. The Farmer’s helpers grabbed him, beat him, and tied him back up. Moral: Be yourself, not someone else.

title: THE MULE
content: A Mule was eating well and getting fat in a nice stable. He kicked up his heels and said, 'My dad must have been a fast racehorse, because I’m so strong!' But the next day, he was put to work carrying heavy loads all day. By night, he was exhausted and said, 'I guess my dad was just a donkey after all.' Moral: Don’t judge yourself by good times alone.

title: THE CAT AND THE BIRDS
content: A Cat heard that some Birds in a cage were sick. She dressed up like a doctor, with a bag of tools, and knocked on their door. 'I’m here to help you feel better,' she said. The Birds replied, 'Thanks, but we’re fine as long as you stay outside.' Moral: Be careful of help from someone who might want to hurt you.

title: THE WOLF AND THE SHEPHERD
content: A Wolf followed a flock of sheep for days, but the Shepherd kept such a good watch that the Wolf couldn’t get one. After a while, the Shepherd got used to seeing the Wolf around and stopped worrying about him. One day, the Shepherd left the flock alone for a bit, and the Wolf attacked, taking off with a sheep. Moral: Don’t trust an enemy just because they hang around.

title: THE FOX AND THE GRAPES
content: A Fox saw some ripe grapes hanging high on a vine. He was hot and thirsty, so he jumped to grab them. He tried again and again but couldn’t reach. Finally, he gave up and walked away, saying, 'They’re probably sour anyway.' Moral: People sometimes pretend they don’t want what they can’t have.

title: THE EAGLE AND THE BEETLE
content: An Eagle was chasing a Hare, who ran to a Beetle for help. The Beetle begged the Eagle to spare the Hare, but the Eagle laughed and ate him anyway. The Beetle didn’t forget. When the Eagle laid eggs in her nest, the Beetle flew up and rolled them out, smashing them. The Eagle was mad and built a higher nest, but the Beetle did it again. Finally, the Eagle gave up. Moral: Even the small can get revenge.

title: THE MICE AND THE WEASELS
content: The Mice and the Weasels were always fighting. The Mice kept losing, so they held a meeting. They decided their leaders needed horns to look important. They made horns out of straw and tied them on. In the next battle, the Mice lost again and ran to their holes. But the leaders with horns couldn’t fit through and got caught by the Weasels. Moral: Looking big doesn’t always save you.

title: THE WOLF AND THE LAMB
content: A Wolf and a Lamb came to a stream to drink. The Wolf stood upstream and the Lamb downstream. The Wolf, looking for an excuse, said, 'How dare you muddy my water!' The Lamb said, 'I can’t, I’m downstream.' The Wolf then said, 'Well, you insulted me six months ago!' The Lamb replied, 'I wasn’t even born then.' The Wolf didn’t care and ate him anyway. Moral: A bully doesn’t need a real reason.

title: THE RAT AND THE ELEPHANT
content: A Rat was walking along when a big Elephant and its fancy parade passed by. The Rat laughed and said, 'Look at me, I’m just as good as that big guy!' A friend said, 'You’re tiny compared to him.' The Rat replied, 'Sure, but I think I’m important too.' Moral: Everyone has their own value, big or small.

title: THE BOYS AND THE FROGS
content: Some Boys were throwing rocks at Frogs in a pond for fun. The Frogs begged them to stop, saying, 'This might be a game to you, but it’s life or death for us.' The Boys just laughed and kept going. Moral: What’s fun for one can hurt another.

title: THE ANT AND THE DOVE
content: An Ant fell into a stream and was struggling to get out. A Dove saw him, dropped a leaf into the water, and the Ant climbed onto it to safety. Later, a Hunter came to catch the Dove with a net. The Ant saw this, bit the Hunter’s foot, and made him yell. The Dove heard and flew away. Moral: One good turn deserves another.

title: THE MAN AND THE SATYR
content: A Man got lost in the woods and met a Satyr, who offered him shelter. It was cold, so the Man blew on his hands to warm them. Later, they ate hot soup, and the Man blew on it to cool it. The Satyr asked, 'How can you blow hot and cold from the same mouth?' The Man said, 'It’s just what I need to do.' The Satyr kicked him out, saying, 'I don’t trust anyone like that.' Moral: People don’t always understand differences.

title: THE HARE AND HIS EARS
content: A Lion got hurt by a Goat’s horns and roared that all horned animals should leave the forest. A Hare, with his long ears, got scared thinking they looked like horns. He ran to a friend and said, 'Should I leave too?' The friend said, 'Your ears aren’t horns.' The Hare stayed but kept worrying. Moral: Don’t let fear trick you.

title: THE FISHERMAN AND THE LITTLE FISH
content: A Fisherman caught a tiny Fish and was about to throw it back. The Fish begged, 'Please let me go, I’m too small to eat. I’ll grow bigger later.' The Fisherman said, 'Maybe, but I’ve got you now,' and kept it. Moral: A little something today is better than a big promise tomorrow.

title: THE WOLF AND THE LION
content: A Wolf stole a sheep and was dragging it away when a Lion showed up and took it from him. The Wolf stood back and grumbled, 'That’s not fair, you took my prize!' The Lion said, 'Did you earn it fairly, or just steal it yourself?' The Wolf had no answer. Moral: Thieves can’t complain about losing stolen goods.

title: THE STAG AND HIS REFLECTION
content: A Stag admired his big antlers in a pool of water, saying, 'These look amazing.' But he hated his thin legs. Then a Hunter came with dogs, and the Stag ran. His legs carried him fast, but his antlers got stuck in some branches, and the dogs caught him. 'If only I’d loved my legs more,' he thought as he fell. Moral: What helps you matters more than what looks good.

title: THE PEACOCK
content: The Peacock bragged about his colorful tail to the other birds. Juno, the goddess, heard him and said, 'You’ve got a nice tail, but can you sing?' The Peacock tried, but his voice was awful. The birds laughed, and Juno said, 'See, everyone has something they’re not good at.' Moral: Don’t brag too much.

title: THE FOX AND THE CROW
content: A Crow sat in a tree with a piece of cheese in her beak. A Fox below wanted it and said, 'You’re so pretty! If you can sing, you’d be perfect.' The Crow, flattered, opened her beak to sing, and the cheese fell. The Fox grabbed it and ran off, saying, 'Thanks for the snack.' Moral: Watch out for flattery.

title: THE HORSE AND THE STAG
content: A Horse owned a field until a Stag came and started eating the grass. The Horse asked a Man for help. The Man said, 'I’ll get rid of the Stag, but you’ll have to let me ride you.' The Horse agreed, and the Man chased off the Stag. But then he kept the Horse as his own. Moral: Trading one problem for a bigger one isn’t smart.

title: THE DOG AND HIS REFLECTION
content: A Dog found a piece of meat and was carrying it home in his mouth. Crossing a stream, he saw his reflection and thought it was another dog with a bigger piece. He dropped his meat to grab the other one, but it sank in the water, and he lost it all. Moral: Don’t lose what you have chasing something you can’t get.

title: THE FOX AND THE STORK
content: A Fox invited a Stork to dinner and served soup in a flat dish. The Fox lapped it up, but the Stork’s long beak couldn’t get any. The Stork invited the Fox back and served soup in a tall jar. The Stork drank easily, but the Fox couldn’t reach it. Moral: Tricks can come back to bite you.

title: THE WOLF AND THE GOAT
content: A Wolf saw a Goat on a cliff and said, 'Come down, the grass is better here!' The Goat replied, 'Thanks, but I know you just want me for dinner.' Moral: Don’t trust advice from someone who might gain from it.

title: THE DOG IN THE MANGER
content: A Dog lay in a manger full of hay, not eating it but barking at the Ox who wanted it. The Ox said, 'Why sit on something you can’t use?' The Dog just growled. Moral: Don’t keep others from what you don’t need.

title: THE BIRDS AND THE BEASTS
content: The Birds and the Beasts were at war. The Bat couldn’t decide whose side to take. When the Beasts were winning, he joined them, saying, 'I’m a Beast, I have teeth!' When the Birds won, he flew with them, saying, 'I’m a Bird, I have wings!' In the end, both sides found out and shunned him. Moral: Pick a side and stick to it.

title: THE BEAR AND THE BEES
content: A Bear smelled honey in a beehive and stuck his paw in to grab some. The Bees stung him hard, and he roared in pain. He swatted at them, but that just made more Bees come out and sting him. Moral: Sometimes it’s better to leave things alone.

title: THE FOX AND THE LEOPARD
content: A Fox and a Leopard argued about who was better. The Leopard said, 'My spots are the prettiest.' The Fox said, 'Maybe, but my brain is smarter than your coat.' Moral: Brains beat looks.

title: THE HERON
content: A Heron stood by a river full of fish. He was picky and waited for a big one. Small fish swam by, but he ignored them. By evening, the big fish were gone, and he had to settle for a tiny one. Moral: Don’t wait too long for something perfect.

title: THE COCK AND THE FOX
content: A Fox saw a Cock in a tree and said, 'Good news! All animals are friends now. Come down and celebrate!' The Cock said, 'Great, I see some dogs coming to join us.' The Fox ran off, and the Cock laughed. Moral: Don’t believe everything you hear.

title: THE DOG AND THE OYSTER
content: A Dog loved eggs and ate them whole. One day, he found an Oyster and swallowed it, thinking it was an egg. His stomach hurt badly after. Moral: Looks can fool you.

title: THE MONKEY AND THE CAMEL
content: At a party, a Monkey danced and everyone clapped. A Camel got jealous and tried to dance too, but he was clumsy and kicked things over. The animals chased him out. Moral: Stick to what you’re good at.

title: THE WOLF AND THE HORSE
content: A Wolf found a field of barley and couldn’t eat it. A Horse came by, and the Wolf said, 'This barley’s great, I saved it for you!' The Horse replied, 'If you could eat it, you wouldn’t be so generous.' Moral: Watch out for fake kindness.

title: THE STAG, THE SHEEP, AND THE WOLF
content: A Stag asked a Sheep to lend him some corn, promising to pay back with a Wolf as his guarantee. The Sheep said, 'The Wolf steals, and you run away. How will I get my corn back?' Moral: Don’t trust shaky promises.

title: THE ANIMALS AND THE PLAGUE
content: A plague hit the animals, and they met to find out who caused it. The Lion said, 'I’ve eaten sheep, but who hasn’t?' The Fox said, 'I’ve stolen chickens, no big deal.' The Donkey said, 'I ate some grass that wasn’t mine.' They all blamed the Donkey and punished him. Moral: The weak often take the blame.

title: THE CAT AND THE OLD RAT
content: A Cat caught lots of Rats until an Old Rat got wise and stayed in his hole. The Cat pretended to be dead to trick him. The Old Rat peeked out and said, 'Nice try, but I’m not coming near you.' Moral: Experience beats tricks.

title: THE FOX AND THE MONKEY
content: A Fox and a Monkey traveled together. The Monkey bragged he was from a noble family. The Fox said, 'My family’s just regular foxes.' When they passed a graveyard, the Monkey said, 'These are my ancestors’ tombs!' The Fox replied, 'Sure, they can’t argue with you now.' Moral: Don’t make up stories that can’t be checked.

title: THE WOLF AND THE SHEPHERDS
content: A Wolf watched some Shepherds eating a sheep in their hut and said, 'They’d be mad if I did that!' Moral: People hate in others what they do themselves.

title: THE SPENDTHRIFT AND THE SWALLOW
content: A young man spent all his money and had only a coat left. He saw a Swallow in early spring and thought summer was here, so he sold his coat. Then it got cold again, and he shivered, saying, 'You tricked me, bird!' Moral: Don’t jump to conclusions.

title: THE TWO TRAVELERS AND THE BEAR
content: Two men were walking when a Bear charged them. One climbed a tree, the other played dead. The Bear sniffed the man on the ground and left. The man in the tree came down and asked, 'What did the Bear say?' 'He said don’t trust friends who run away,' replied the other. Moral: True friends stick around in trouble.

title: THE HARE AND THE TORTOISE
content: A Hare laughed at a Tortoise for being slow and said, 'I could beat you in a race any day!' The Tortoise said, 'Let’s try it.' They started, and the Hare sped ahead but stopped to nap, thinking he had time. The Tortoise kept going and passed him. When the Hare woke up, the Tortoise had won. Moral: Slow and steady wins the race.

title: THE PORCUPINE AND THE SNAKES
content: A Porcupine asked some Snakes if he could share their den. They said yes, but when he moved in, his sharp quills poked them every time he turned. They asked him to leave, but he said, 'I like it here.' Moral: Bad guests make life hard.

title: THE FOX AND THE PHEASANTS
content: A Fox saw some Pheasants in a tree and wanted to eat them. He danced and acted crazy below them. They watched, confused, until one flew down to see. The Fox grabbed it and ate it. Moral: Don’t fall for distractions.

title: THE MOON AND HER MOTHER
content: The Moon asked her Mother to make her a dress. Her Mother said, 'How can I? You change size every night!' Moral: Some things can’t be pinned down.

title: THE LARK AND HER YOUNG ONES
content: A Lark built a nest in a wheat field. As the wheat grew, her Young Ones asked, 'When do we leave?' She said, 'When the farmer says it’s time to cut.' The farmer came and said, 'I’ll ask my neighbors to help.' The Lark stayed calm. Then he said, 'I’ll do it myself tomorrow.' The Lark told her kids, 'Now we go.' Moral: Rely on yourself, not others.

title: THE ASS AND HIS DRIVER
content: An Ass was being driven down a hill but stopped at the edge of a cliff. The Driver pulled him back, but the Ass wouldn’t move and fell off. Moral: Stubbornness can lead to ruin.

title: THE LION AND THE FOX
content: A Fox laughed at a Lion for having only one cub. The Lion said, 'Yes, but he’s a lion.' Moral: Quality beats quantity.

title: THE CAT, THE COCK, AND THE YOUNG MOUSE
content: A young Mouse came home and told his mother he met two animals. One was gentle with soft fur, the other loud with a sharp beak. His mother said, 'The gentle one’s a Cat who’d eat you, the loud one’s a Cock who’s safe.' Moral: Looks can be deceiving.

title: THE WOLF AND THE SHEEP
content: A Wolf bit a Sheep but got hurt and couldn’t hunt. He asked the Sheep for water, saying, 'You hurt me, so help me now.' The Sheep said, 'No, you hurt me first.' Moral: Don’t expect help from those you’ve harmed.

title: THE FIGHTING COCKS AND THE EAGLE
content: Two Cocks fought over the farmyard. The winner crowed on the roof, but an Eagle swooped down and took him. The loser stayed safe below. Moral: Pride can lead to a fall.

title: THE OLD LION AND THE FOX
content: An old Lion couldn’t hunt anymore and pretended to be sick in his den. Animals came to visit, and he ate them. A Fox came but stayed outside, saying, 'I see tracks going in but none coming out.' Moral: Learn from others’ mistakes.

title: THE BUTTERFLY AND THE ROSE
content: A Butterfly fell in love with a Rose and kept flying around her. The Rose said, 'I’ll fade soon, and you’ll move on.' Sure enough, the Rose withered, and the Butterfly found another flower. Moral: Love doesn’t always last.

title: THE CRAB AND HIS SON
content: A Crab told his Son, 'Walk straight, not sideways.' The Son said, 'You show me.' The Crab tried but walked sideways too. Moral: Lead by example.

title: THE WOLF AND THE HOUSE DOG
content: A Wolf met a fat House Dog and asked, 'How do you get so much food?' The Dog said, 'My master feeds me, but I wear a collar.' The Wolf said, 'I’d rather be free and thin.' Moral: Freedom is worth more than comfort.

title: THE EAGLE AND THE KITE
content: An Eagle asked a Kite to marry him, saying, 'I’m strong and brave.' After the wedding, he couldn’t catch food and grew weak. The Kite left him. Moral: Don’t trust big promises.

title: THE LION, THE BEAR, AND THE FOX
content: A Lion and a Bear fought over a deer they both caught. They battled until they were too tired to move. A Fox came by, took the deer, and left them there. Moral: Fighting can let someone else win.

title: THE HEN AND THE FOX
content: A Fox tried to trick a Hen by saying, 'Your chicks are so cute, let me see them!' The Hen said, 'Nice try, but I know you.' Moral: Don’t fall for sweet talk.

title: THE LION AND THE MOUSE
content: A Lion caught a Mouse but let him go when the Mouse begged. Later, the Lion got trapped in a net. The Mouse heard him roar, chewed the ropes, and set him free. Moral: Small friends can help big ones.

title: THE CROW AND THE PITCHER
content: A thirsty Crow found a pitcher with water too low to reach. She dropped pebbles in until the water rose high enough to drink. Moral: Little efforts can solve big problems.

title: THE ANT AND THE GRASSHOPPER
content: An Ant worked all summer storing food while a Grasshopper played. When winter came, the Grasshopper was hungry and asked for help. The Ant said, 'You should’ve worked like me.' Moral: Prepare for tough times.

title: THE FOX AND THE GOAT
content: A Fox fell into a well and couldn’t get out. A Goat came by, and the Fox said, 'The water’s great, jump in!' The Goat did, and the Fox climbed on him to escape, leaving the Goat stuck. Moral: Look before you leap.

title: THE SHEEP AND THE PIG
content: A Sheep and a Pig were caught by a Butcher. The Pig squealed loudly, but the Sheep stayed quiet. The Pig asked, 'Why aren’t you scared?' The Sheep said, 'He’ll just take my wool, but he wants your meat.' Moral: Fear depends on what’s at stake.

title: THE FARMER AND THE STORK
content: A Farmer set a net and caught some Cranes eating his crops, along with a Stork. The Stork begged, 'I’m not a Crane, I was just here!' The Farmer said, 'You’re with them, so you’re guilty too.' Moral: Who you hang out with matters.

title: THE GNAT AND THE BULL
content: A Gnat landed on a Bull’s horn and said, 'Sorry if I’m heavy!' The Bull said, 'I didn’t even notice you.' Moral: Don’t overestimate yourself.

title: THE FROGS WHO WISHED FOR A KING
content: Some Frogs asked for a king. A Log fell into their pond, but they complained it did nothing. Then a Stork came as their king and ate them. Moral: Be careful what you wish for.

title: THE OWL AND THE GRASSHOPPER
content: An Owl was sleeping when a Grasshopper sang loudly and woke her. She asked him to stop, but he kept going. She waited until night and ate him. Moral: Respect others’ peace.

title: THE DONKEY AND THE LOAD OF SALT
content: A Donkey carried a load of salt and fell into a stream. The salt melted, making the load light. Next time, he fell on purpose. His owner then loaded him with sponges, which got heavy when wet, and the Donkey learned his lesson. Moral: Tricks can backfire.

title: THE LION AND THE ASS
content: A Lion and an Ass went hunting. The Ass brayed to scare animals toward the Lion, who caught them. The Ass said, 'I helped a lot!' The Lion said, 'Yes, but I’d eat you if you weren’t my friend.' Moral: Know your place.

title: THE MONKEY AND THE DOLPHIN
content: A Monkey fell off a ship and a Dolphin saved him, thinking he was a man. The Monkey said he was from a great city. The Dolphin asked, 'Do you know Piraeus?' The Monkey said yes, and the Dolphin, realizing he lied, let him drown. Moral: Lies can sink you.

title: THE WOLF AND THE ASS
content: A Wolf caught an Ass and said, 'I’ll eat you now.' The Ass said, 'Wait, I’ve got a thorn in my foot—pull it out first.' The Wolf tried, and the Ass kicked him hard and ran off. Moral: Quick thinking can save you.

title: THE MONKEY AND THE CAT
content: A Monkey and a Cat found some chestnuts in a fire. The Monkey said, 'You pull them out, you’ve got paws!' The Cat did, burning herself, while the Monkey ate them all. Moral: Don’t let others use you.

title: The Red Shoes
content: Karen was a poor girl who lived with her mom in a tiny house. One day, a kind shoemaker felt sorry for her bare feet and made her a pair of bright red shoes. They weren’t just any shoes—they sparkled like rubies and fit her perfectly. Karen loved them so much she couldn’t stop looking at them. She wore them everywhere, even to church, where her mom said they were too fancy. People whispered and pointed, but Karen didn’t care. She twirled her feet under the pew, smiling to herself. The next day, something strange happened. Karen put on the red shoes to walk to the market, and suddenly her feet started moving on their own. They skipped, then danced, pulling her down the street past the baker’s shop and the blacksmith. 'Stop!' she shouted, but her feet kept going. Kids ran after her, laughing, while Karen’s face turned pink with worry. Soon, she was dancing out of town, into the fields where the grass was tall and scratchy. She grabbed a fence to stop, but the shoes yanked her free. They danced her into the woods, over rocks and roots, splashing through a cold stream. The sun went down, and still she danced, her legs shaking and her breath short. 'Help me!' she cried, but only the wind answered. By morning, she was deep in the forest, her red shoes dusty but still shining. An old lady with a cane saw her spinning by a little cottage. 'What’s wrong, child?' she asked. Karen panted, 'These shoes won’t stop dancing!' The lady frowned. 'Magic shoes,' she said. 'They’re cursed to dance forever unless you cut them off.' She handed Karen a pair of rusty scissors from her apron. Karen’s hands shook as she bent down. The shoes fought, kicking high, but she snipped the laces one by one. With a final snap, they fell off, lying still in the dirt. Karen’s feet stopped at last, and she fell to her knees, hugging the old lady. 'Thank you,' she whispered. The lady nodded. 'Take them home, but never wear them again.' Karen carried the red shoes back in her arms, her bare feet sore but free. She locked them in a wooden box under her bed and never opened it. From then on, she wore plain brown boots and was happy just to walk where she wanted. She’d learned that pretty things can sometimes lead you into big trouble if you’re not careful.

title: The Headless Horseman
content: Ichabod Crane lived in Sleepy Hollow, a quiet town surrounded by dark woods. Everyone there told stories about a headless horseman—a ghost who rode at night looking for his lost head. Ichabod was a skinny schoolteacher with a big nose, and he always laughed at those tales. 'Just old gossip,' he’d say. But one foggy night, everything changed. He’d been at a party, eating pie and singing songs, and rode home late on his old horse, Gunpowder. The road was shadowy, with trees bending low like claws. Halfway home, he heard a thud-thud-thud behind him. He turned and saw a rider in the mist—no head on its shoulders, just a black cape flapping. Ichabod’s stomach dropped. 'Go, Gunpowder!' he yelled, kicking the horse hard. The old nag galloped toward the covered bridge where folks said the ghost couldn’t follow. The hoofbeats got louder, closer, and Ichabod’s hat flew off as he clung to the saddle. He glanced back—the horseman held a round thing in his hand, like a ball. Then it flew through the air and smashed into Gunpowder’s side. It was a pumpkin, orange and mushy, and the horse stumbled. Ichabod tumbled off, rolling into wet bushes. He peeked out, heart pounding like a drum. The rider stopped at the bridge, laughed a deep, empty laugh, and raised another pumpkin high. Ichabod ducked, waiting for it to hit, but then the hoofbeats faded. He crawled to the bridge and saw nothing but fog. Shaking, he ran home, locked his door, and stayed up all night with a candle burning. The next day, kids found his hat by the bridge next to a smashed pumpkin. Ichabod told everyone what happened, his voice wobbly. 'I saw him—the headless horseman!' Nobody laughed anymore. From then on, Ichabod took the long road home, avoiding that bridge. He never forgot the thud of those hooves or the pumpkin that nearly got him, and he stopped calling those old stories silly.

title: The Golden Goose
content: Dummling was the youngest of three brothers, and they all thought he was slow. One day, their dad sent them to chop wood in the forest. The older brothers packed big lunches and left Dummling with just a crust of bread. In the woods, he met a little old man with a gray beard. 'Can I have some food?' the man asked. The older brothers had said no, but Dummling smiled and shared his crust. 'You’re kind,' the man said. 'Chop that tree over there—you’ll find something special.' Dummling grabbed his axe and chopped the tree down. Out popped a goose with feathers made of gold, shining like the sun. He picked it up, and it stuck to his hands—magic! He didn’t mind and walked toward town with it under his arm. People stared as he passed, the goose glowing bright. A nosy innkeeper’s daughter saw it and thought, 'I’ll take a feather!' She grabbed it, but her hand stuck to the goose. She yelled, 'Let go!' but couldn’t pull free. Then a priest walked by and tried to help her. He touched her shoulder and stuck too. A farmer saw the fuss and grabbed the priest’s coat—stuck! Soon, Dummling was leading a line of people stuck together, all shouting and tripping over each other. He kept walking, grinning at the silliness. They passed a castle where a princess lived who never smiled. She looked out her window, saw the goofy line—Dummling with his golden goose, the girl, the priest, the farmer—and burst out laughing. Her dad, the king, heard her and ran out. 'You made my daughter laugh!' he said. 'That’s been my wish for years. Keep the goose as your reward.' Dummling bowed, and the king clapped his hands. The stuck people popped free, rubbing their hands and muttering. The princess came down, still giggling, and thanked Dummling. He took the golden goose home, and it laid golden eggs sometimes. His brothers were jealous, but Dummling shared the gold with them anyway. He’d learned that being kind could turn a crust of bread into a treasure, and he was happy with that.

title: The Singing Bone
content: Once there were two brothers, Hans and Karl, who lived near a dark forest. A wild boar was wrecking the king’s fields, and he promised gold to whoever killed it. Hans was brave and good, but Karl was sneaky and mean. They set out together with spears and a horn. Deep in the woods, Hans spotted the boar—huge, with tusks like knives. He threw his spear and hit it square in the side. The boar squealed and fell, dead. Hans wiped his brow and said, 'We’ll share the gold.' But Karl’s eyes narrowed. He didn’t want to share. While Hans bent to clean his spear, Karl crept up and pushed him into a deep ditch. Hans yelled, but Karl covered the hole with dirt and rocks, leaving him buried. Karl dragged the boar to the king, blowing the horn loud. 'I killed it!' he lied. The king gave him a sack of gold, and Karl went home smirking. Years passed, and a shepherd found a white bone in that ditch. It was Hans’s rib, clean and smooth. He carved it into a flute and played it. But when he did, the bone sang: 'My brother killed me for gold, buried me deep, took my prize—tell the king!' The shepherd’s jaw dropped. He ran to the castle and played the flute for the king. The bone sang again, clear and sad. The king’s face turned hard. 'Bring Karl here,' he ordered. Soldiers grabbed Karl from his house, where he’d been counting his gold. They dragged him to the king, and the shepherd played the flute once more. 'My brother killed me...' it sang. Karl’s face went white. 'It’s a trick!' he shouted, but the king didn’t listen. 'You buried your own brother,' he said. 'Take him away.' Karl was locked in a tower, and the gold was given to the poor. The shepherd kept the singing bone, and sometimes folks heard it hum in the wind near that ditch. Hans was gone, but his story lived on, warning everyone that greed could dig a hole you can’t climb out of.

title: The Brave Little Tailor
content: A little tailor sat in his shop one sunny day, stitching a shirt. He’d bought some jam and spread it on bread, but flies buzzed around it. Annoyed, he swatted seven with one smack. 'Seven at one blow!' he cheered. He sewed that onto his belt and decided to show the world how brave he was. He left town with just his belt and a piece of cheese in his pocket. On the road, he met a giant picking apples. 'Hey, little man,' the giant laughed, 'what’s with the belt?' The tailor puffed up. 'I killed seven at one blow!' The giant smirked. 'Prove it—squeeze water from this rock.' The tailor pulled out his cheese, squeezed it, and whey dripped out. The giant blinked, impressed. 'Okay, throw this stone farther than me,' he said, hurling one over a hill. The tailor picked up a bird from a bush, tossed it, and it flew out of sight. 'Beat that!' he said. The giant scratched his head. 'Come work for me,' he said. They went to the giant’s cave, where another giant waited. That night, they gave the tailor a huge bed. He didn’t trust them, so he slept in a corner. Good thing—the giants smashed the bed with clubs, thinking he was dead. Morning came, and the tailor popped up, whistling. 'Nice try!' he said. The giants ran off, scared. Next, the tailor reached a kingdom where a mean bear was loose. The king said, 'Catch it, and you’ll get my daughter.' The tailor found the bear in a field, eating honey. He danced around it, singing loud, until the bear chased him to a tree. He climbed up, dropped a rock, and bonked the bear’s head. It fell asleep, and he tied it up with thread. The king laughed when he saw it. 'You’re small but mighty!' The tailor married the princess and lived in the castle, his belt still bragging 'Seven at one blow.' He never told anyone it was flies, not giants or bears, and everyone called him the bravest man around.
